quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the words used when sizing up a warping and sizing department.

questions.q: A warper's beam normally carries which part of the warp?
options: A creel-full of ends, one of several beams combined later at sizing
The weft yarn for the loom
The sized warp ready for the loom
questions.explain: A warper's beam holds as many ends as the creel has cones; several such beams are combined on the sizing machine into the weaver's beam. The sized warp ready for the loom is the weaver's beam, not the warper's.

questions.q: The 'yards per shift at 100 %' figure is theoretical; the actual output is that figure multiplied by the efficiency.
questions.explain: The drum never runs for the whole shift — creel changes, breaks and doffing stop it — so the theoretical yards are scaled by the efficiency to get what is actually warped.

questions.q: Which machine combines several warper's beams into a single weaver's beam?
questions.explain: The sizing creel holds the set of warper's beams and the sizing machine runs them together through the size box onto one weaver's beam. The warper only makes the individual beams.

questions.q: 'Creel capacity' of a warper means
options: the number of cones the creel holds, which caps the ends per warper's beam
the weight of yarn a cone holds
the number of beams the sizing creel holds
the number of looms one warper can feed
questions.explain: One end comes from each cone, so the creel's cone count fixes the most ends a warper's beam can carry; the beam count on the sizing creel is a separate limit.

questions.q: A warp contraction of 10 % means the sized warp length needed per day is
options: the same as the fabric length
questions.explain: Warp yarn crimps as it interlaces, so more warp length is consumed than fabric is produced: 100,000 m of fabric needs 110,000 m of warp. Dividing by 1.10 is the reverse error.

questions.q: The circumference of the warping drum is π × diameter, and each revolution winds one circumference of yarn.
questions.explain: A 30-inch drum has a circumference of π × 30 = 94.25 in, which is the yarn length drawn forward per revolution.

questions.q: Why must the warper produce ten beam-lengths for every one sized beam in Problem 2?
options: The sizing machine runs ten times faster
Each warper's beam carries only one-tenth of the 8,064 ends
Ten per cent is lost as warp contraction
The looms run in ten-hour shifts
questions.explain: Total ends ÷ creel capacity gives ten beams per set; each must be warped to the full length, so the warper runs ten times the sized length. Contraction is a separate 10 % that was already applied to the sized length.

questions.q: The result '1.27 warpers required' is best read as
options: the plant needs two warpers, or one warper with a larger creel
the plant needs one warper running 27 % overtime forever
the figure should be rounded down to one warper
the sizing machine is the bottleneck
questions.explain: Fractional machines cannot be bought; the lecture suggests two warpers, or one with a larger creel so fewer beams per set are needed. Sizing came out at 1.02, so it is not the bottleneck.

questions.q: In the drum-speed worksheet, the efficiency figure accounts for
options: time lost to creel changes, end breaks and beam doffing
the difference between yards and metres
the thickness of yarn on the beam
questions.explain: Efficiency is running time as a fraction of shift time; it has nothing to do with unit conversion or yarn shrinkage.

questions.q: 'Yarn to be warped per day (m of beam)' in Problem 2 counts
options: the length run on the warper with each beam of the set counted separately
the length of yarn on all cones
questions.explain: The warper has to run every beam of the set to the full length, so the daily warping requirement is sized length × beams per set: 110,000 × 10 = 1,100,000 m of beam.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Which formula, which direction — the relationships behind the three worksheets.

questions.q: Yards per hour of a warping drum are given by
questions.explain: Inches per hour = rpm × 60 × circumference, and 36 inches make a yard. Omitting the 60 gives yards per minute; omitting π uses the diameter instead of the circumference.

questions.q: If the drum diameter is doubled at the same rpm, the yards warped per shift
options: rise by a factor of π
questions.explain: Circumference is proportional to diameter, so every revolution winds twice the length and output doubles.

questions.q: The time to fill a beam is
questions.explain: At 100 % the time is length ÷ speed; dividing by the efficiency as well stretches it to the real time including stops. Ignoring efficiency is the common mistake.

questions.q: Convert a warping speed of 900 m/min to yards per minute (1 m = 1.0936 yd). Give the answer to the nearest yard.
questions.explain: 900 × 1.0936 = 984.2, so about 984 yd/min — the speed used in Problem 1.

questions.q: The weight of yarn on a beam in pounds is
questions.explain: Total yarn length in yards divided by the yards per pound (840 × Ne) gives pounds. Multiplying by 840 × Ne is the reversed formula.

questions.q: For the same ends and beam length, a coarser yarn (lower Ne) gives a heavier beam.
questions.explain: Weight = yards ÷ (840 × Ne); a smaller Ne in the denominator means more pounds. Ne 20 yarn weighs 1.5 times as much as Ne 30 for the same length.

questions.q: Sized warp needed per day equals
questions.explain: Warp is longer than the fabric it makes, so the fabric length is inflated by the contraction: 100,000 × 1.10 = 110,000 m.

questions.q: Warper's beams per set are found by
options: total ends ÷ creel capacity, rounded up to a whole number
questions.explain: 8,064 ends with a creel of, say, 840 cones gives 9.6, which must be rounded up to 10 because a tenth beam is needed for the leftover ends.

questions.q: If sizing efficiency falls from 75 % to 60 % with all else unchanged, the sizing machines required (1.02) become about
questions.explain: Daily capacity is proportional to efficiency, so the requirement scales by 75 ÷ 60 = 1.25: 1.02 × 1.25 ≈ 1.28. Dividing the other way gives the wrong 0.82.

questions.q: Enlarging the warper creel reduces the number of warpers needed for the same loom shed.
questions.explain: A bigger creel means fewer beams per set, so fewer beam-lengths are run for each sized beam and the warper's daily workload falls.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Work through the drum, the beam and the 200-loom shed with the figures from the lecture.

questions.q: A warping drum of 30 in diameter runs at 300 rpm. How many inches of yarn does it draw forward per hour? Use π = 3.1416.
questions.explain: Revolutions per hour = 300 × 60 = 18,000; circumference = π × 30 = 94.25 in; 18,000 × 94.25 ≈ 1,696,460 in per hour.

questions.q: Convert 1,696,460 inches per hour to yards per hour, to the nearest yard.
The drum makes 47,124 yd per hour. How many yards are warped in an 8-hour shift at 80 % efficiency, to the nearest hundred yards?
A beam of 20,500 yd is warped at 984 yd/min with 64 % efficiency. How many minutes does it take to fill?
The beam carries 800 ends, each 20,500 yd long. How many yards of yarn are on the beam?
questions.explain: Total yarn = ends × length = 800 × 20,500 = 16,400,000 yd.

questions.q: 16,400,000 yd of Ne 30 cotton yarn is on the beam. What does the yarn weigh, to the nearest pound?
200 looms each weave 500 m per day and the warp contraction is 10 %. How many metres of sized warp are needed per day?
A sizing machine runs at 100 m/min with 75 % efficiency, 24 hours a day. How many metres can it size per day?
The fabric is 63 in wide with 128 ends per inch. How many ends are in the warp?
questions.explain: Total ends = EPI × width = 128 × 63 = 8,064. 7,560 is 120 × 63 and 8,192 is a creel-sized round number, both wrong.

questions.q: 1,100,000 m of beam must be warped per day and one warper makes 864,000 m per day. Warpers required?
questions.explain: 1,100,000 ÷ 864,000 = 1.27. The reverse division gives 0.79, and 1.02 is the sizing-machine figure.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Decisions a preparatory department manager has to make with these numbers.

questions.q: The calculation gives 1.27 warpers. Which is the least costly way to avoid buying a second warping machine?
options: Enlarge the creel so fewer beams are needed per set
questions.explain: A bigger creel cuts beams per set (10 → 8 with 1,008 cones), cutting the warper's daily metres to 880,000 and the requirement to about 1.02. Slowing the looms wastes loom capacity.

questions.q: Sizing came out at 1.02 machines. What is the sensible response?
options: Install a second sizing machine at once
Lift sizing efficiency or speed by a few per cent so one machine copes
Reduce the number of looms to 190
Ignore it — 1.02 rounds to one machine
questions.explain: A 2 % shortfall is within reach of a small efficiency gain (77 % instead of 75 % is enough); a second machine for 2 % of capacity would sit idle. Simply ignoring it builds up a shortage of warp.

questions.q: Warping efficiency is well below 100 % mainly because
options: the drum slows as the beam fills
the creel must be re-loaded with cones and ends pieced up between beams
the sizing machine stops the warper
questions.explain: Creel changes, end breaks and doffing the full beam are stop time; the drum speed itself is set and does not fall as the beam fills.

questions.q: Because each loom weaves 500 m of fabric a day, the sizing department should plan to size exactly 500 m of warp per loom per day.
questions.explain: Warp contraction means 500 m of fabric consumes 550 m of warp at 10 % contraction; planning on fabric length leaves the looms short of warp.

questions.q: A full beam of 651 lb exceeds the safe lift of the mill's beam trolley. The practical remedy is to
options: put more ends on the beam
questions.explain: Weight is ends × length ÷ (840 × Ne); shortening the beam reduces it directly. A coarser count or more ends would make it heavier.

questions.q: If the drum speed is pushed far above the rated rpm, the first thing that happens is
options: more end breaks and uneven tension, so efficiency falls
questions.explain: Higher speed raises tension peaks and breaks; the extra stops can cancel the speed gain. Yards per revolution depend only on the drum diameter.

questions.q: The mill decides to warp 15,000 yd beams instead of 20,500 yd. At 984 yd/min and 64 % efficiency, how many minutes does one beam take?
Which single input has the largest effect on the warpers required in Problem 2?
options: Beams per set, fixed by the creel capacity
questions.explain: Beams per set multiplies the whole daily warping length (×10 here); the other inputs change it only proportionally or not at all.

questions.q: The shed is expanded to 300 looms of the same quality. Sizing machines required become about
questions.explain: Requirement scales with looms: 1.02 × 300 ÷ 200 = 1.53, so two sizing machines are now needed.

questions.q: Changing the quality from 128 to 60 ends per inch on the same 63 in width and 840-cone creel halves the beams per set and so the warper's daily workload.
questions.explain: 60 × 63 = 3,780 ends ÷ 840 = 4.5 → 5 beams instead of 10, so the warper runs 5 beam-lengths per sized beam instead of 10.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder mixed questions across the lecture, including the mistakes students make most often.

questions.q: A drum of 32 in diameter runs at 350 rpm for an 8-hour shift at 85 % efficiency. Yards warped per shift, to the nearest hundred?
A student divides 20,500 yd by 984 yd/min and reports 20.8 min to fill the beam. What has been forgotten?
questions.explain: 20.8 min is the 100 % time; dividing by 0.64 gives the real 32.5 min. Ends do not affect the time, only the weight.

questions.q: A beam of 2,000 ends, 15,000 yd long, in Ne 20 weighs about
A set is 10 warper's beams, each with 800 ends of Ne 30 yarn and 20,500 yd long. What is the total yarn weight of the set, to the nearest 10 lb?
The warper must run ten times the sized length because each warper's beam carries only one-tenth of the ends.
questions.explain: 8,064 ends ÷ 840 cones = 9.6 → 10 beams; each is warped to the full length, so the warper does ten beam-lengths per weaver's beam.

questions.q: With a 1,008-cone creel the 8,064 ends fit on 8 beams. The daily warping requirement becomes
questions.explain: 110,000 m sized × 8 beams = 880,000 m of beam per day. 864,000 is one warper's capacity, not the requirement.

questions.q: With 880,000 m of beam to warp per day and 864,000 m per warper per day, how many warpers are required? Give two decimals.
questions.explain: 880,000 ÷ 864,000 = 1.019 ≈ 1.02 — one warper can almost cope once the creel is enlarged.

questions.q: A planner sizes exactly 100,000 m per day for 200 looms weaving 100,000 m of fabric, yet the looms keep running out of warp. The reason is
options: the sizing machine is too slow
warp contraction — the looms consume about 110,000 m of warp for 100,000 m of fabric
the warper creel is too small
questions.explain: Warp crimp means every metre of fabric uses about 1.1 m of warp; sizing only the fabric length leaves a 10 % shortfall every day.

questions.q: Which pair of drums gives exactly the same yards per hour?
options: 150 rpm at 60 in and 300 rpm at 30 in
150 rpm at 30 in and 300 rpm at 60 in
300 rpm at 15 in and 150 rpm at 60 in
100 rpm at 30 in and 300 rpm at 20 in
questions.explain: Speed is proportional to rpm × diameter: 150 × 60 = 300 × 30 = 9,000. The other pairs give different products.

questions.q: What warping speed in metres per minute does a 30 in drum give at 300 rpm? (1 m = 39.37 in; π = 3.1416.)
